content.text: This chapter teaches two tools that help Linux administrators manage storage more efficiently:
Stratis — manages storage and lets file systems grow as needed.
VDO (Virtual Data Optimizer) — helps save disk space by reducing duplicate data and compressing data.
Think of normal storage as a box with a fixed size. These tools help you manage that space more flexibly.
Stratis is a storage management tool for Linux. It combines storage devices into a pool and creates file systems from that pool.
Imagine you have two 5 GB disks:
You can create a file system from the pool without manually managing every low-level storage detail.
Pool: A group of storage capacity managed together.
File system: The structure Linux uses to store and organize files.
Thin provisioning: A file system can appear larger than the physical storage currently used for it. Actual disk usage increases as data is written.
Snapshot: A saved view of a file system at a particular point in time. It can help you access earlier versions of files.
These examples follow the RHEL 8 textbook. They may need adjustments on RHEL 10.
stratisd is the background service that manages Stratis.
stratis-cli provides the commands you type to manage Stratis.
Start the service now and enable it to start automatically after reboot:
Warning: The following examples assume /dev/vdb and /dev/vdc are empty, dedicated lab disks. Never use a disk containing important data.
pool create creates a storage pool.
/dev/vdb is the disk assigned to the pool.
This adds /dev/vdc to labpool, increasing its available physical storage.
List the devices in the pool:
Remember: A pool groups storage together; adding a disk increases the pool's capacity.
Create a file system named labfs inside labpool:
sudo stratis filesystem create labpool labfs
Create a directory to use as the mount point:
Here, df -h displays file-system space in an easy-to-read format.
A manual mount may not return automatically after reboot. To make it persistent, add this entry to /etc/fstab:
systemctl daemon-reload asks systemd to reload its configuration.
mount -a attempts to mount file systems configured in /etc/fstab.
Always check for errors before rebooting.
Suppose your Stratis file system is allowed to grow to a large logical size, but it initially contains only a small amount of data.
It does not need to consume all that physical storage immediately. Actual physical usage grows as you write data.
Physical storage is used as data grows.
You can manage growing storage needs more easily.
Important: Thin provisioning does not create unlimited physical disk space. You must monitor the real storage pool so it does not run out of space.
A snapshot gives you a point-in-time view of a file system. It can help recover a file that was deleted after the snapshot was taken.
sudo stratis filesystem snapshot labpool labfs labfs-snap
List the file systems and snapshots:
Remember that a snapshot is not a substitute for a separate backup. If the underlying storage fails, the snapshot may be lost too.
VDO stands for Virtual Data Optimizer.
Its purpose is to reduce the amount of physical storage used by data through two techniques:
Deduplication: Recognizes duplicate data and avoids storing repeated copies unnecessarily.
Compression: Stores data in a form that takes less space when the data can be compressed.
Imagine you store the same large file three times. Without deduplication, each copy could use additional disk space. With deduplication, VDO can recognize the repeated data and save space.
The vdo package provides VDO management commands. kmod-kvdo provides the required kernel module for that RHEL 8 environment.
The commands in this section are specifically from the RHEL 8 book. VDO availability and management differ across RHEL versions, so check your installed RHEL version before trying them.
Warning: Creating a VDO volume on a device can overwrite or repurpose storage metadata. Use only a dedicated, disposable lab disk.
The textbook example creates a volume named vdo1 on /dev/vdd, with a logical size of 50 GB:
vdo create creates a VDO volume.
--vdoLogicalSize=50G sets the logical capacity presented to users.

The logical capacity can be larger than the actual physical disk. This is called thin provisioning. It requires careful monitoring because the physical disk can fill up before the logical capacity is reached.

The output includes information such as:
Size: Logical size presented by the VDO device.
Use%: Percentage of physical space used.
Space saving%: Estimated storage saved through VDO.
When you copy a file to the VDO volume, physical usage can increase. Copying the same file again may use much less additional space because VDO can recognize duplicate data.
Do not assume that every file will compress well or contain duplicates. The savings depend on the data.
Forgetting to start or enable stratisd.
Using a disk that contains important data.
Forgetting to make the mount persistent in /etc/fstab.
Assuming thin provisioning means unlimited storage.
Confusing logical size with physical storage usage.
Expecting VDO to save the same amount of space for every type of file.
Forgetting that snapshots are not full backups.

Stratis makes it easier to combine storage, create file systems, expand pools, and take snapshots.
VDO reduces physical storage usage through deduplication and compression.
Thin provisioning lets logical storage capacity exceed the physical space currently consumed, but physical capacity must still be monitored.
/etc/fstab helps make mounts persistent across reboots.
Always practise storage commands on dedicated lab disks, never on a disk containing important data.
